Infinite realms of immortals and impossibilities, the Outer Planes brim with celestials, fiends, gods, and the dead—and they're all just a step away. Enter a portal to Sigil, the City of Doors—an incredible metropolis where portals connect to every corner of the multiverse. From there, venture to the Outlands, the hub of the Outer Planes, and discover wonders beyond imagination, as well as the secrets of celestials, fiends, gods, and the dead. ''Planescape: Adventures in the Multiverse'' contains everything a Dungeon Master needs to run adventures and campaigns set in Sigil and the Outlands, as well as new options for players who want to create characters prepared to explore the planes.}} ==Contents== * "[[Planescape: Adventures in the Multiverse/Sigil and the Outlands|Sigil and the Outlands]]", a 96-page hardcover book that includes player options as well as details on Sigil, the [[Outlands]], and the [[gate-town]]s. * "[[Planescape: Adventures in the Multiverse/Turn of Fortune's Wheel|Turn of Fortune's Wheel]]", a 96-page hardcover adventure set in Sigil and the Outlands for levels 3–10. * "[[Planescape: Adventures in the Multiverse/Morte's Planar Parade|Morte's Planar Parade]]", a 64-page hardcover book with stats and descriptions of creatures found in the Outer Planes. * Double-sided poster map showing both Sigil and the Outlands. * Sturdy, four-panel Dungeon Master's screen. {{-}} ==Appendix== === Background Information === * Although the scant Planescape material in 3rd and 4th seemed to follow on the same timeline as 2nd Edition, it's uncertain where 5e's ''Adventures in the Multiverse'' fits into the timeline, if anywhere. It may be a reboot, or given how many plane-shaking events happen during the life of Dungeons & Dragons, there may be reality-alteration at play. ** Evidence indicating a continued timeline: *** The [[Mind's Eye]] faction: it came into existence as a result of the [[Faction War]]. The text even indicates it's the result of a merging of two previous factions. *** [[Jeremo]] the Natterer ({{b|Planescape|In the Cage: A Guide to Sigil|pdf=17274}}) claims he wants to bring the [[Ring-Givers]] into Sigil as a full faction, with plans to take over from Factol [[Ingwe]]. Here, the Ring-Givers are a minor faction, with Jeremo listed as factol. His earlier headquarters, the [[Palace of the Jester]], is mentioned as having been sold by the Ring-Givers. *** The [[Tower Sorcerous]] has recently returned to Sigil. *** The [[Grixitt]] ({{b|Planescape|Uncaged: Faces of Sigil|pdf=17285}}) has been captured and imprisoned. *** The events of ''Turn of Fortune's Wheel'' are a direct result of the events of the 2e {{b|Planescape|The Great Modron March|pdf=17302}} adventure. ** Evidence indicating a reboot of some sort: *** The factions are in Sigil with no suggestion that they were ever kicked out. Factions and factols may have returned, but even factols who were killed in the Faction War (e.g. [[Hashkar]]) are back. *** The structure of many faction headquarters is inconsistent with their original appearance. *** [[Morte Rictusgrin]] appears in the ''Turn of Fortune's Wheel'', evidently waiting for [[The Nameless One|someone]] in the [[Mortuary]], suggesting it takes place before the events of {{b|Torment|Planescape: Torment}}. ''Torment'' takes place in [[125 YFHR]], just before 2nd Edition's books. ===External Links=== {{External link disclaimer}} * {{FRW}} * {{DMsGuild|Planescape: Adventures in the Multiverse (Roll20 VTT)}} * {{DriveThruRPG|Planescape: Adventures in the Multiverse (Roll20 VTT)}} ===Connections=== [[Category:Planescape sourcebooks]] [[Category:5th edition sourcebooks]] [[Category:Boxed sets]] [[Category:Published in 2023]]

{{Plane | image = | caption = | name = Pocket Plane | othernames = | demonym = | natives = | languages = | basicrefs = | type-GW = [[Demiplane]] | shape-size-GW = | gravity-GW = Normal | time-GW = | morphic-GW = | element-energy-GW = | alignment-GW = | magical-GW = | layers-GW = | layer-number-GW = | location-GW = [[Throne of Blood]] | refs-GW = <ref name="BG.SoA"/><ref name="BG.ToB"/> | type-WA = | shape-size-WA = | gravity-WA = | mutability-WA = | element-energy-WA = | alignment-WA = | magical-WA = | layers-WA = | layer-number-WA = | location-WA = | refs-WA = | type-WT = | shape-size-WT = | gravity-WT = | time-WT = | morphic-WT = | element-energy-WT = | alignment-WT = | magical-WT = | faith-WT = | layers-WT = | layer-number-WT = | location-WT = | refs-WT = | inhabitants = | deities = | locations = | organizations = | settlements = | usethe = | useon = }} The '''Pocket Plane''' was a [[demiplane]] that was formed as plane-within-a-plane of [[Bhaal]]'s divine realm, the [[Throne of Blood]]. It was an aspect of the final destination that faced all of [[Bhaalspawn|Bhaal's mortal children]] after their deaths.<ref name="BG.SoA">{{Cite game/Baldur's Gate II: Shadows of Amn}}</ref><ref name="BG.ToB">{{Cite game/Baldur's Gate II: Throne of Bhaal}}</ref>
The plane was believed to have been formed by the will of the [[Bhaalspawn]] [[Abdel Adrian]], to safeguard his mind and shield him from Bhaal's complete power.<ref name="BG.ToB"/>
==Description== The plane was a smaller version of Bhaal's Throne of Blood. It comprised a central area with a large stone gate, known as the ''Gate of the Watchers''.<ref name="BG.ToB"/> Extending off the main chamber were five smaller passages leading to smaller, enclosed areas.<ref name="BG.SoA"/>
When the Pocket Plane first appeared, the gate was surrounded by eyes of different colors.<ref name="BG.SoA"/> In its later iteration the eyes were absent and each of the smaller passages were closed off by some manner of supernatural barrier. These barriers could be bypassed upon the completion of several trials.<ref name="BG.ToB"/>
Beyond the ''Gate of the Watchers'' was a passageway that took Abdel "where he needed to be" and was capable of connecting to the [[Mana Forge]] in the Throne of Blood.<ref name="BG.ToB"/>
==Cosmography== This plane was referred to as being a part of [[Hell]]<ref name="BG.SoA"/> but also [[Abyss]]al in nature. It was in fact a part [[Bhaal]]'s ream of the [[Throne of Blood]],<ref name="BG.ToB"/> which at the time was adrift in the [[Astral Plane]].<ref name="F&A-p45">{{Cite book/Faiths & Avatars|45}}</ref>
==Inhabitants== Although the plane was readily accessible by Abdel Adrian, it was also the temporary home to two other individuals. One of the residence was an unnamed [[solar]] who was tasked to watch over and guide Abdel through the [[Bhaalspawn crisis]]. The second was an [[imp]] by the name of [[Cespenar]], who once served as a "butler" to Bhaal.<ref name="BG.ToB"/>
==History== The first confirmed existence of the plane occurred in the {{YearlinkName|1369}}. While it existed beforehand,<ref name="BG.SoA"/> it was believed to have been significantly shaped by the simultaneous deaths of Abdel Adrian and Jon Irenicus, the latter of whom who had stolen most of Abdel's divine soul.<ref name="BG.ToB"/>
During the plane's first iteration, each of its chambers held a different trial that was put for to Abdel Adrian on their path to self-discovery. These were tests of fear, selfishness, greed, pride and wrath; during which he faced several demons, an imprisoned [[genie]] in the possession of the famed ''[[Blackrazor]]'', and a [[wraith]]-like apparition of [[Sarevok#Existence After Death|Sarevok]]. Upon the completion of each trial, Abdel received one of the ''[[Tears of Bhaal]]'' which could be used to close one of the gate's eyes.<ref name="BG.SoA"/>
After closing the final eye, Abdel was confronted by Irenicus one last time. The exiled [[mage]] appeared in the form of Bhaal's [[avatar]], the [[Slayer]]. The fought once again, but ultimately Abdel was able to claim his soul back and return to [[Toril]] on the [[Prime Material plane]].<ref name="BG.SoA"/>
The ''Pocket Plane'' appeared again when Abdel slew another individual who possessed part of Bhaal's divine essence." This person was [[Illasera|Illasera the Quick]], one of the actual Bhaalspawn.<ref name="BG.ToB"/>
Abdel was greeted by his guardian Solar, who in turn presented him with an apparition of Sarevok. Abdel's half-brother had been in Bhaal's realm for some time and sought to live a mortal life once again.<ref name="BG.ToB"/>
Under the direction of [[Amelyssan the Blackhearted]], Abdel confronted the other Bhaalspawn of [[the Five]]. Every time he slew another member of [[the Five]], Abdel was transported back to the Pocket Plate and presented with another challenge. Upon the death of all members of the Five, Abdel was forced to destroy the Pocket Plane and face Amelyssan at the Mana Forge in Bhaal's Throne of Blood.<ref name="BG.ToB"/>

'''Polyhedron''' was one of several official magazines published to support [[Dungeons & Dragons]], in this case is was part of the benefits for membership in the Role-Playing Game Association.
''Polyhedron'' launched five years after ''[[Dragon]]'' and five years before ''[[Dungeon]]'', in 1981. It was published quarterly until 1982, bimonthly until 1991, monthly until [[1996]], and then bimonthly until May 2003. It was published in even-numbered months (February, April, June, August, October, December) while ''Dungeon'' appeared in odd-numbered months (January, March, May, July, September, November).
From 2002 to 2004, ''Polyhedron'' was merged with ''Dungeon'', with individual issues being dual-numbered: Dungeon #90 and Polyhedron #149 are the same magazine. After 2004, the ''Polyhedron'' content was dropped.
== Planescape Content == === 2nd Edition === * October [[1994]]: {{b|Polyhedron|Polyhedron Magazine 100}} ** '''Cover''': [[James Halloway]] depicts the [[Lady of Pain]] playing cards and observing a bar brawl. ** '''The Analects of Sigil''': [[Monte Cook]] describes a scholar searching for the Five Citadels of Surrender on the negative side of the Inner Planes. Although the citadels are different, this may be the inspiration for what became the four Citadels of the [[Doomguard]] bordering on the [[Negative Energy plane]].
* December [[1997]]: {{b|Polyhedron|Polyhedron Magazine 127}} ** '''Cover''': ''Have a Holly Jolly, Berk.'' [[Rob Lazzaretti]] depicts the encounter from the [[Day of Grace]] article. ** '''The Day of Grace''': [[Monte Cook]] describes an event in [[Sigil]]'s history between a young girl and the [[Lady of Pain]] which began the annual holiday known as the Day of Grace (or simply "Grace"). The timing of the article (and cover caption) suggest it's Sigil's version of Christmas.
* December [[1998]]: {{b|Polyhedron|Polyhedron Magazine 133}} ** '''Stench Kine Recipes!''': [[William James Cuffe]] offers stats on the [[stench kine]] as well as two related recipes.
* April [[1999]]: {{b|Polyhedron|Polyhedron Magazine 135}} ** '''Gifts from Below''': [[Erik Mona]] offers a look at some magic items from the planes. Planar-themed, but not Planescape-specific.
* August [[1999]]: {{b|Polyhedron|Polyhedron Magazine 137}} ** '''Of Sigil and the Sea''': [[William James Cuffe]] provides a tour of the [[Ditch]], the most prominent "waterway" in [[Sigil]].

{{Polyhedron magazine | image = Polyhedron100.png | caption = | issue = 100 | volume = 15, No 10 | publisher = [[TSR, Inc.]] | editor = [[Jean Rabe]] | cover_artist = [[James Holloway]] | edition = 2 | month = October | year = 1994 | previous = | next = [[Polyhedron Magazine 127|''Polyhedron'' #127]] | source = [https://archive.org/details/Polyhedron155/polyhedron%20100/page/n1/mode/2up ''Polyhedron'' #100 at archive.org] }}
'''''Polyhedron'' issue 100''' was released in October of 1994. It contained the following articles related to Planescape:
== Cover == The cover depicts, among other things, the [[Lady of Pain]] playing cards, watching a bar brawl.
: Artist [[James Holloway]] aptly penned his rendition of a celebration over our 100th issue. The Network member who creates the most interesting AD&D® Game NPC from among the characters pictured will win the original piece of art. Deadline: December 15, 1994. Best of luck!
== Analects of Sigil: The Five Citadels of the PLANESCAPE Setting == : ''By [[David Cook|David "Zeb" Cook]], artwork by [[Tony DiTerlizzi]].'' '''p. 6-7'''
The article is presented as the confessions of [[Handulus]], scholar of the third rank, as extracted by the [[Mercykillers|Mercykiller]] [[Jerak]]. Handulus is under arrest for the murder of his mentor, Factor [[Jeron]].
Handulus describes five citadels found on the [[Inner Planes]], the [[Five Citadels of Surrender]]. He'd found some hints about then in the ''[[Grand Dictum]]'', and then found a single page from the ''[[Codex of Infinite Planes]]''. He likens them to the four [[Doomguard]] citadels. Each of the five citadels is a stop on a journey, with one leading to the next.
# The [[Great Mine]] in the [[Quasi-Elemental Plane of Salt]], through which you must surrender your fear. # The [[Embracing Tower]] in the [[Quasi-Elemental Plane of Ash]], through which you must surrender your hope. # The [[Invisible Labyrinth]] in the [[Quasi-Elemental Plane of Vacuum]], through which you must surrender compassion. # An unnamed citadel in the [[Quasi-Elemental Plane of Dust]], through which you lose all remorse. # The final citadel is in the [[Negative Energy plane]]. Handulus didn't visit that one.
Handulus admits he didn't kill Jeron, but Jeron is still surely dead, as Handulus had shown him his notes on the citadels. Because Jeron had departed to explore all five citadels. And without fear, hope, compassion, or remorse, what remains to be taken?
==Appendix== === Background Information === * The article title is misleading: ** An "analect" is a series of short philosophical or literary extracts. The title isn't exact; the article itself is such an extract, but not a collection of them. ** While the extract is "of Sigil," the citadels described are found on the [[Inner Planes]]. * Handulus mentions the "Governors." This presumably refers to the Guvners, the nickname of the [[Fraternity of Order]]. This may be the only time that "Governors" is used in reference to them. * This article is the first appearance of the term [[factor]] to refer to a faction rank.

{{Item | image = portal 4e.jpg | caption = ''A portal to someplace else.'' | name = ''Portal'' | othernames = | nicknames = | type = | location = | value1e = | weight1e = | refs1e = | school2e = | level2e = | value2e = | weight2e = | refs2e = | school3e = Strong [[transmutation]] (while functioning)
Weak [[transmutation]] (while not functioning) | casterlevel3e = | itemlevel3e = | value3e = | weight3e = | refs3e = {{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Setting 3rd edition|59}} | level4e = | value4e = | weight4e = | refs4e = | rarity5e = | attunement5e = | school5e = | level5e = | value5e = | weight5e = | refs5e = | communication = | languages = | alignment = }} '''Portals''' were permanent teleportation effects that linked many places in and outside [[Abeir-Toril|Toril]], including other planes and planets.{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Setting 3rd edition|59}} {{Quote |Ah, yes, spellspun gates. Portals, some call them. "Death-doors" is the term I prefer. The reason? Well, each step through one is a step closer to the time when your death is standing waiting for you on the other side—with a big cold grin on its face and a sword in its hand you'll have no time nor chance to avoid. |[[Bharajak Steelshar]]{{Cite book/Hand of Fire}} }} ==Description== [[File:Portal.JPG|250px|thumb|''A transparent portal gave off information about its destination.'']] A ''portal'' was a two-dimensional, often up to {{SI|15|ft|long=yes}} circle, but not limited to it both in size and shape, area that was both intangible and invisible. Due to this, a freestanding archway of some kind usually was built to identify the location of a ''portal'', so those who could not [[detect magic|detect magical auras]] did not stumble into them accidentally. It was impossible to visually find out a ''portal's'' destination. For example, sticking one's head into that field to find out the destination was impossible, for touching a ''portal'' activated it. One way to find out the location of a ''portal'' was to cast ''detect magic''. The magical aura of a functional ''portal'' was much stronger than that whose uses were completely exhausted. Finding out more about a ''portal'' required an ''[[analyze portal]]'' [[spell]]. The portal itself was completely intangible. ''[[Portal finder]]s'' were tools to find ''portals''.{{Cite book/Underdark|72}} A ''[[greater Underdark map]]'' also had the location of every ''portal'' within the mapped area.{{Cite book/Underdark|77}} Passing through a portal was described as an unsettling experience: space between the "fabric of the planes" was entirely dark, devoid of air and offering no sensation of temperature. Oddly enough, it seemed to elicit phantom scents, like the smell of wintergreen or stale [[wine]].{{Cite book/The Adversary/Hardcover|172}} ==Powers== ''Portals'' were magical transportation devices. When somebody touched the two-dimensional field, that person was affected by a ''[[greater teleport]]'' effect towards a pre-set destination. This was the reason why the "sticking the head through"-method to find out the destination failed. Creatures could enter and be transported by a ''portal'', as long as they could pass through them, and objects could not. For example, one could not shoot arrows through a ''portal'', they would not just not pass through, but bounce off. An exception to this no-object-rule were those objects carried by creatures passing through a ''portal''. However, even this had a limit of 850 pounds (386 kilograms) and the definition of "carried" was anything touched. This weight limit had the peculiarity that an object that was touched by several creatures dropped the amount of objects the creatures could carry by its weight for all and not just for one. The limit on how many creatures could pass through a ''portal'' was the one that the builder set and the usual limit was as many creatures as wanted to pass through. A ''portal'' could only send a person to its destination, but not back. Quite often, people built directly at the destination a second ''portal'' to effectively create a two-way-''portal''. Destroying a ''portal'' was very difficult. ''[[Disintegrate]]'' or other physical means were not means by which a ''portal'' could be destroyed. Successfully using ''dispel magic'' could stop the working of a ''portal'' for up to twenty four seconds. It required a ''[[Mordenkainen's disjunction]]'' spell to turn a ''portal'' permanently non-functional. Another means was the ''[[gate seal]]'' spell. A tool to manipulate and glean information from ''portals'' was a ''[[staff of portals]]''.{{Cite book/Underdark|72}} A tool to destroy a ''portal'' was a ''[[portal demolisher]]''.{{Cite book/Underdark|75}} ===Special Portals=== There were some special types of ''portals'': ;Creature-Only ''Portals'':Creature-only ''portals'' were what they sounded like. Only creatures could pass through them, their clothes or other equipment could not, those simply stayed behind while the body moved on.{{Cite web/Perilous Gateways/One-Way Portals in Amn:The Dusty Rat}} A variety that was hard to create allowed both creatures and equipment to pass through the same ''portal'', but the body and equipment reached different destinations. ;Keyed ''Portals'':It happened quite often that ''portals'' were keyed. This meant that the created ''portal'' could only be used if a special condition was met. Such conditions could be ones that needed to be met by the user, like being a member of a specific race, or ones that needed to be met otherwise like specific time. Keyed ''portals'' needed to be activated and remained so for six seconds. Once activated, anybody could use it during its activation by touching the ''portal'', even without fulfilling the criteria.{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Setting 3rd edition|60}} For example, the [[Ched Nasad portal]] could only be activated by [[drow]] who were male and not divine spellcasters. When it came to the surface end, it was only possible to activate it while [[the sun]] was set.{{Cite web/Perilous Gateways/Dark Elf Portals: The Ched Nasad Portal}} A tool that allowed a person to activate any keyed ''portal'', even without knowledge of its key, was a ''[[universal key]]''.{{Cite book/Underdark|76}} ;Impassable ''Portals'':Impassable ''portals'' were not passable for anything. An impassable ''portal'' differentiated from most ''portals'' in that it could be used like a window to the destination nobody could reach, while normal ''portals'' gave off no information about its destination. ;Nonliving-Only ''Portals'':A nonliving-only ''portal'' was one that allowed only nonliving material through. It was the only type of ''portals'' that allowed nonliving things to pass through without a living creature carrying it.{{Cite book/Underdark|52}} ;Random ''Portals'':A random ''portal's'' randomness lay in its activation time. It was random and even when a person hit upon a random ''portal'' that was in its activation time, it could be impossible to use, because one lacked the proper key. There was one pattern for a random ''portal'' that was quite common. It was one that worked for a random number of creatures between seven and twelve and once the random number went through the ''portal'' stopped working for a random time up to six days. ;Transparent ''Portals'':Transparent ''portals'' were ''portals'' whose destination could be seen.{{Cite book/Underdark|52-53}} ;Variable ''Portals'':Variable ''portals'' were ''portals'' with more than one set destination. These ''portals'' were considered dangerous to those who were not familiar with them. The reason was that the multiple destinations could change according to a pattern or at random depending on how they were created. A possible danger, which aforementioned people with no familiarity could encounter was that the ''portal'' was set to transport a person with the proper key to the actually intended destination while sending people without the proper key to a dangerous location like the inside of a volcano. ===Malfunction=== [[File:Bar the Gate.jpg|thumb|right|300px|''An adventurer closing a ''portal'' opened by the [[Cult of the Dragon]].'']] A ''portal's'' magic was very durable, but it was subject to wear. ''Portals'' could also be influenced by global magical catastrophes. Such ''portals'' started to malfunction. Malfunctioning ''portals'' were generally a century or older. When such a malfunctioning continuous ''portal'' was activated, the ''portal'' could start to show its malfunctions and applied such effects for up to a minute. Possible malfunctions were that the ''portal'' did not apply a ''greater teleport'' but a ''[[greater dispel magic]]'' effect to either the user or the user's [[magic item]]s. When the former happened, the target was the user and could lose magical effects he or she was benefiting from. When the latter happened, what the ''portal'' did was draining the magic items of magic to power itself, the magic items stopped working for a short time, when it came to charge-based magic items, they lost charges. Another effect that could happen was that the user was shoved off as though he or she suffered a ''[[telekinesis]]'' effect. Another possible effect was that the ''portal'' spilled either and ''[[inflict serious wounds]]'' or ''[[cure serious wounds]]'' out against the user.{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Setting 3rd edition|61}} Even when the ''portal'' sent somebody off, it could send somebody to a wrong place. However, about half the time, a ''portal'' worked properly and one could further stabilize it with a ''[[portal stabilization]]'' spell{{Cite book/Underdark|60}} or by applying special ''portal''-related stabilization skills. ;''Portal'' Seepage:''Portal'' seepage was an occurrence that accompanied malfunctioning ''portals''. It happened when ''portals'' grew old and their magic started to deteriorate. ''Portal'' seepage happened often to malfunctioning ''portals'' that were more than a millennium old and was an often encountered problem in the [[Lowerdark]]. When this occurred, qualities of the ''portal's'' destination such as planar qualities affected the origin point as well.{{Cite book/Underdark|53, 120}} ==Creation== The creation of a ''portal'' was formerly believed to require specific ''portal''-knowledge, but it turned out that they could be created by anybody who could create [[:Category:Wondrous items|wondrous items]]. However, having specific knowledge still helped to cut the costs of creation by half.{{Cite book/Player's Guide to Faerûn|42}} The creation required one of the following spells: ''[[teleport]]'', ''greater teleport'', ''[[teleportation circle]]'', or ''[[gate]]''. It was also a very costly process. A default ''portal'', meaning one-way, always active, and of 10 feet (3 meters) radius, cost 50,000 [[gp]], a large part of the creator's personal essence, and one hundred days. When creating a ''portal'', the creator needed to set a destination. Any place could be this destination, as long as it fulfilled two criteria. First, it needed to be a place where the creator had been at least once. Second, it needed to be a place where travel via the [[Astral Plane]] was possible, this was due to the nature of teleportation spells in general. As mentioned above, a so called two-way ''portal'' was actually not one ''portal'' but two ''portals'', one being built on the other's destination point. Creating a second ''portal'' on the destination point cost half the amount of money to create the first one, more personal essence, and fifty days or more in time. As mentioned above, a standard ''portal'' was created with a 10 feet (3 meters) radius, but could be as small as 6 inches (15 centimeters) in radius. As a rule of thumb, ''portals'' that were bigger than the aforementioned 10 feet in radius cost more for every 300 square feet fraction by another 100% in monetary cost. Turning a ''portal'' into an impassable one or keying and randomizing a ''portal'' incurred no additional costs, but adding more destinations than one increased the cost by a fourth for every additional destination, when it came to creature-only ''portals'', the cost was actually doubled. Those creature-only ''portals'' that sent equipment and body to different destinations incurred costs like a creature-only ''portal'' with one additional destination and were very costly. When it came to nonliving-only ''portals'', the cost was four times as high as a normal one. Turning a ''portal'' transparent cost a flat 50,000 gp. The creation of a ''portal'' with limited number of usages was a cost-saving measure. A continuously active portal and one that could be used five times per day cost the same. It cost less as less frequently the ''portal'' could be used. A portal could be created to work even less frequently than once per day dropping the cost even further, but this had a limit. A portal that allowed travel once a tenday was the limit, ''portals'' that worked even less frequently could be still created, there was simply no saving regarding the costs. ==Reputation== A lot of people created ''portals'' in Toril's history. Due to the durable nature of this [[magic]], Toril had ''portals'' in the hundreds by [[1372 DR]]. However, quite often, the purpose and usage instructions went lost over time alongside their creators. Therefore, ''portals'' were considered both mysterious and unpredictable. {{fq | float = right | width = 255px | source = Graffiti on a ''portal'' to the [[Elemental Plane of Fire]] | text = Don’t forget the marshmallows! }} ''Portals'' existed throughout the [[Underdark]]. Entire networks were the primary means people moved around in the Realms Below. Such a ''portal's'' location was often made clear by means of archways, columns, or simple stone piles, if it was part of a trade route. A site with a ''portal'' often had graffiti carved or written. Graffiti provided from time to time information about the ''portal's'' nature or its destination, albeit not always in a clear manner. One group of people who sought the destruction of interplanar ''portals'' were the [[incantatrix|incantatar]]s. They did not want creatures from foreign planes to enter their own and as such viewed it as their duty to destroy as many interplanar connections as possible. That said, they were a font of knowledge for ''portals'' in general.{{Cite book/Player's Guide to Faerûn|61}} The existence of spells developed by mages from other planes like ''[[Otto's irresistible dance]]'' or ''[[Tenser's transformation]]'' was accredited to interplanar ''portals''.{{Cite book/Player's Guide to Faerûn|140}} ==Notable Portals== {{Quote|''It's amazing that Faerûn holds together, considering how it's been riddled with gates and conduits, portals and doorways from a dozen lost peoples. If I had anything like a sense of wonder I might be impressed.''|[[Eidola]] of [[Neverwinter]]{{Cite book/Easy Betrayals|41}}}}
===Elfgates=== The elfgates were portals that could teleport things to and from [[Evermeet]]. ;[[Elion]] to [[Evereska]]: One side of this gate was on a hill about a mile above the palace of [[Seiveril Miritar]] near Elion in northern Evermeet. It was in a broad glade and consisted of three old stone markers.{{Cite book/Forsaken House|197}} The other side was a plaza in Evereska.{{Cite book/Forsaken House|199}} ;[[Moonwood]] to [[Evereska]]: The Evereskan side of this gate lay high in the northern [[Shaeradim]] surrounding Evereska, and consisted of a stone marker covered in [[Espruar]] runes beside a waterfall beneath a stone cliff. The other side of the gate linked to a northerly outpost of [[Sharrven]] before it became a ruin.{{Cite book/Forsaken House|232-233}} ===Bukhara Spires=== {{Main|Bukhara Spires}} These were teleportation spires created by the [[Imaskari]].{{Cite book/The Grand History of the Realms|18}} ===Elemental Vortices=== [[Elemental vortices]] were pathways connecting [[elemental planes]] with one another{{Cite book/Secrets of the Lamp/Genie Lore|10}} or the [[Prime Material Plane]].{{Cite book/Planescape Campaign Setting/A DM Guide to the Planes|20-21}} ===Shadow Portals=== A shadow ''portal'' was a naturally occurring ''portal'' like one of the vortices. The difference was that it did not connect to one of the [[Inner Planes]] but to the [[Shadowfell]]. Technically, these were simple planar holes towards the Shadowfell and not ''portals'', but they worked like ''portals''. About four-fifths of them were two-way ''portals'' and the other one-fifth were one-way ''portals'' They were always active and did not need to be specifically activated. They were a specific feature of the Lowerdark and were more common the deeper one went.{{Cite book/Underdark|120}} ===Time Gates=== Much rarer than normal portals, a few [[time gate]]s existed throughout Faerûn. They were physically similar to other portals, but transported an individual not through space, but into a different time.{{Cite book/Cormanthyr: Empire of the Elves|6}} ===Weavegates=== A weavegate looked and behaved similarly to a regular portal, unless the user knew how to navigate the [[Weave]]. For such users, the weavegate could be used to reach any other portal reached by the Weave, instead of the pre-set destination. Traveling in this way gave the sensation of gently falling through a glowing blue void.{{Cite web/theedverse/2022-06-30 - Weavegate to RenFaire}} ==Appendix== ===See Also=== * [[Perilous Gateways]]: A webseries that featured portals found across [[Faerûn]]. * [[Elemental vortex]] ===Appearances=== :;Novels ::''[[The Glass Prison]]'' •''[[Sentinelspire (novel)|Sentinelspire]]'' • ''[[The Fanged Crown]]'' • ''[[The Adversary]]'' ===References=== {{Refs}} [[Category:Magic items]] [[Category:Wondrous items]] [[Category:Items from the Underdark]] [[Category:Items]] [[Category:Items from Toril]] [[Category:Items from Faerûn]] [[Category:Planar pathways]]

After the [[Spellplague]], the Positive Energy plane collapsed into the [[Elemental Chaos]], mixing with all the other Inner Planes.{{Cite book/Forgotten Realms Campaign Guide|66}} Cosmologists believe that [[positive energy]] and its opposite [[negative energy]], combined with the four elements, make up the known universe.{{Cite book/Dungeon Master's Guide v.3.5|148}} This plane was a continuous explosion of energy not meant for mortals. Despite its nickname, the Plane of Life could bring swift death to the unprotected by filling them with positive energy until their cells burst and they joined the conflagration. ==Cosmology== According to the Great Wheel cosmology model, the Positive Energy plane could be reached via the [[Ethereal Plane]] or an adjacent elemental plane, but ''not'' by an elemental vortex. If traveling through the Deep Ethereal, a pure white ''curtain of vaporous color'' indicated the boundary of the Plane of Life's Border Ethereal region.{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 1st edition|12}} Such was the power of the Positive Energy plane that the boundary with the Border Ethereal was weak and fluctuated randomly at times. Travelers thinking they were safe staying in the Border Ethereal could suddenly be dumped on the Plane of Life some distance from the rapidly receding border. Using the [[Great Wheel cosmology#Basic Structure|spherical model]], this plane was adjacent to the quasi-elemental planes of [[Quasielemental Plane of Mineral|Minerals]], [[Quasielemental Plane of Radiance|Radiance]], [[Quasielemental Plane of Lightning|Lightning]], and [[Quasielemental Plane of Steam|Steam]].{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 1st edition|52}} Temporary gates could be created by the ''[[plane shift]]'' spell.{{Cite book/Player's Handbook 2nd edition|224}} As described by the World Tree cosmology model, the [[Astral Plane]] connected all planes with the [[Prime Material Plane]] and the Ethereal Plane was only used for journeying between locations on the Prime.{{Cite book/Dungeon Master's Guide v.3.5|147}} The Positive Energy plane was not connected or coterminous with any other elemental plane.{{Cite book/Dungeon Master's Guide v.3.5|150}} The spell ''[[astral projection]]'' {{Cite book/Dungeon Master's Guide v.3.5|151}}{{Cite book/Player's Handbook v.3.5|201}} could be used to reach the Positive Energy plane via a shining white ''color pool''.{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 3rd edition|49}} Additionally, the ''[[gate]]'' {{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 3rd edition|33}}{{Cite book/Player's Handbook v.3.5|234}} and ''[[plane shift]]'' {{Cite book/Player's Handbook v.3.5|262}} spells could be used to open a temporary portal to this plane. ==Description== {{quote |It is power incarnate.
It is radiance beyond compare.
It is life realized to the fullest. |[[Manual of the Planes 3rd edition|Manual of the Planes]] }} Both the [[Great Wheel cosmology|Great Wheel]] and [[World Tree cosmology|World Tree]] cosmological models were in nearly complete agreement about the nature of this plane, describing it as an infinite, empty, blinding firestorm of life-giving light, but object proof that too much of good thing can kill you—quickly. Upon entering this plane, an unprepared traveler would have first noticed the sun-like brilliance burning into her eyes, severely limiting the range of vision and only being able to discern nearby beings or objects by the shadow they made in the backdrop of infinite dazzle. As she gasped at a sight not meant for mortal eyes, she would have quickly realized there was no breathable atmosphere to even form a scream. The sudden feeling of weightlessness might not have been cause for concern because almost immediately any wounds would have been healed as the life-giving energy permeated her entire being and then went beyond any sense of wellness she had ever experienced. Infused with power only felt in dreams, she might have briefly entertained the thought that air was no longer necessary as she ascended to godhood, but as her cells reached their capacity, she would have realized in a fleeting moment what it means to be mortal before exploding in a burst of [[radiant energy]]. In any infinite plane there is room for variation and the Positive Energy plane was no exception. The ebb and flow of energies created zones that could be classified as [[Planar traits#Elemental and Energy Traits|minor-positive dominant]] as well as places that detonated with concentrated bursts even more intense than the usual activity. Matter from other planes could sometimes be found in the more stable minor-positive dominant areas and some were even inhabited, but there was the constant danger that an energy surge could overwhelm an area without warning. Travelers were advised to have some form of [[positive energy protection]] ready at all times because even brief exposure to the raw energy of this plane could be fatal. There were reports that the life energy would even seep into the possessions of visitors, occasionally imbuing them with a form of life both animated and aggressive. A small biting coin purse might not pose much of a threat, but an angry helmet squeezing your favorite head could be quite a distraction. The rapid healing and boosting properties of this plane drew the very desperate and the very ambitious to attempt exposing themselves to the life-giving energy for just the right amount of time to gain the benefits and not pay the ultimate price. Those that succeeded in exiting the plane or removing themselves from the radiation in time would be completely healed of all wounds and their supercharged bodies could withstand more damage than usual. This effect lasted anywhere from a few minutes up to about three hours, after which all things returned to normal. Note that the Positive Energy plane has no effect on disease because the energy helps the disease as much as the victim. Healing also does not prevent thirst, starvation, or suffocation. ==Inhabitants== Inhabitants were extremely rare on this plane. The only creatures known to inhabit the Plane of Life were the mysterious [[outsider]]s, the [[xag-ya]], and [[ravid]]s. Constructs such as [[golem]]s and other things that do not benefit from healing could exist here without detrimental effects. ==Appendix== ===Further reading=== For possible (non-canon) inhabitants of the [[Quasielemental Plane of Radiance]], see: * {{Cite dragon | author = [[Bennet Marks]] | editor = [[Matthew Sernett]] | title = Creatures of Brilliance: Inhabitants of the Plane of Radiance | issue = 321 | date = July 2004 | pages = {{{1|70-75}}} }} ===External Links=== * {{FRW}} ===References=== {{Refs}} ===Connections=== {{Cosmologies}} [[Category:Inner Planes]] [[Category:Energy planes]] [[Category:Great Wheel planes]] [[Category:World Tree planes]] [[Category:Planes of existence]]

The '''powers''' are a term used by [[planar]]s to refer to the gods of the Outer Planes, although it sometimes also refers to other incredibly powerful beings, like the [[Lords of the Nine]], who are nonetheless not typically considered gods.
Although she technically qualifies, the [[Lady of Pain]] is rarely considered a power, probably due to superstitious reasons: associating her with the powers may be too close to worship for many Cagers, and no one wants to be thrown to the [[Maze]]s.
The powers are one of the alliterative groups used to represent the denizens of the planes: [[prime]]s, [[planar]]s, [[petitioner]]s, [[proxy|proxies]], and powers.
Gods typically organize themselves into pantheons, where each pantheon is worshipped by a particular culture, race, or entire Prime world.
In terms of puissance, sages recognize several tiers: near-powers, demi-powers, lesser powers, intermediate powers, and greater powers.

== Deep History ==
The multiverse was swirling chaos. Forms coalesced, creating the planes and the first [[power]]s.
Two of the powers championing the forces Law were the [[Twin Serpents]]: [[Jazirian]], a winged and feathered serpent dedicated to Good, and [[Ahriman]], a scaled serpent dedicated to evil. The ring formed by two biting each others' tails demarcated a new plane called the [[Outlands]], and other planes fell in around it, forming the [[Great Ring]] of the [[Outer Plane]]s. This action also enshrined the [[Unity of Rings]] as a fundamental multiversal law.<ref name="gth2">{{b|D&D|Guide to Hell|pdf=17390|page=2}}</ref>
In honor of the triple aspects of Law, Good, and Evil, the Serpents established the [[Rule of Three]]. The Serpents attempted to define a center for the multiverse. Despite the advantage of the Outlands, Jazirian pushed for [[Mount Celestia]], while Ahriman pushed for the inverted mountain of [[Baator]].
The two tore themselves apart in their disagreement, with both fleeing to their respective preferred planes. Jazirian bled from her tail, the tip torn off. Wherever drops landed, a [[couatl]] was born. Wingless Ahriman fell to the deepest pit of Baator, and wherever he bled, a [[baatezu|devil]] arose. The lack of a defined center paradoxically gave rise to the third multiversal law, the [[Center of All]].
Weakened in their struggle, other powers usurped them, founding pantheons and spreading their influence across the planes.<ref name="gth3">{{b|D&D|Guide to Hell|pdf=17390|page=3}}</ref>
Ahriman rebranded himself as [[Asmodeus]], lord of [[Nessus]], a near-[[power]] at best, although he secretly remained a Greater Power.<ref name="gth48">{{b|D&D|Guide to Hell|pdf=17390|page=48}}</ref>

The '''Primals''' are a [[sect]] mostly found on the Inner Planes. No one knows much about about them, as they remain very secretive. One can surmise from the "Primal" name and their base of operations that it has something to do with the elemental planes as the building blocks of the multiverse.
== History ==
== Philosophy ==
Other than whatever their core philosophy might be, Primals often say "power told is power lost," explaining their profound secrecy. Whatever they've found, or are looking for, they don't want to share it with anyone.
== Role ==
== Membership ==
Presumably anyone willing to explore the elements and also keep a secret is welcome to join. Potential initiates go through a long screening process and probationary period, but the criteria for admission remain a mystery.
The first rank are ''initiates''. Those who apply themselves may become ''lorewardens''. The third and final rank is ''loremaster'', a title held by extremely few.
Members can never leave the Inner Planes.

A '''prime''' is a creature born on the [[Prime Material plane]]. Often called [[Outsider (Prime)|Outsider]]s, or more derogatorily, "Clueless," although that depends on the prime. Getting to the planes generally requires a certain degree of power, even if they have some strange ideas in their heads, so primes are afforded some amount of respect.
Most primes encountered on the planes are adventurers, there for a specific task, and will likely return home once their job's done. Others are trapped, or take a liking to their new surroundings, and set up a permanent home in the planes.
Primes have some qualities that planars do not:
* Primes have a [[silver cord]] in the [[Astral Plane]], tracing their way back to their bodies left behind on the Prime Material. * Primes are completely immune to planar magic, like ''protection from evil'' or ''monster summonings''.
"Prime" is also sometimes used as a shorthand for the Prime Material Plane, but in such cases, the word is capitalized: e.g. "a ''prime'' comes from the ''Prime''."

I sure hope you know what the Prime is, because it's an essential part of planar knowledge." | source = Kiarus Thorntongue, Smoldering Corpse Patron in [[Sigil]]{{Cite game/Planescape: Torment}} }}A few early versions of the Great Wheel cosmology, as well as the [[World Tree cosmology]],{{Cite book/Player's Guide to Faerûn|139-140}} considered that there was an infinite number of material planes, among them [[Toril]]'s Material Plane, [[Oerth]]'s material plane, [[Krynn]]'s material plane, and the universe in which [[Earth]] was located.{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 1st edition|117}} In the World Tree cosmology, Toril's Material Plane was the main hub that connected all the planes of the cosmology.{{Cite book/Dungeon Master's Guide 5th edition|44}} For that reason, travel between planes was almost exclusively done via passing through the Material Plane first. ''[[Portal]]s'' were rumored to exist that connected Toril to other material planes, using conduits that passed through the [[Plane of Shadow]]. In the [[World Axis cosmology]], the Material Plane, more usually called "the mortal world",{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 4th edition|7}} existed between the two opposing [[fundamental plane]]s: the Astral Plane, commonly called the Astral Sea, and the [[Elemental Chaos]]. == Known Worlds == The Prime Material Plane was known to be home to: * [[Aebrynis]] (the homeworld of the ''Birthright'' setting) * [[Athas]] (the homeworld of the ''Dark Sun'' setting) * [[Krynn]] (the homeworld of the ''Dragonlance'' setting, found in [[w:c:spelljammer:Krynnspace|Krynnspace]]) * [[Mystara]] (the homeworld of the ''Mystara'' setting) * [[Oerth]] (the homeworld of the ''Greyhawk'' setting, found in [[w:c:spelljammer:Greyspace|Greyspace]]) * [[Toril]] (the homeworld of the ''Forgotten Realms'' setting, found in [[w:c:spelljammer:Realmspace|Realmspace]]) * Other worlds, such as: ** [[Gith (world)|Gith]], the original home of the [[githyanki]] and [[githzerai]] people ** [[Glemayne]] ** The unnamed world on which can be found the [[Io's Blood Isles]] archipelago ** [[Logicus]] ** [[Neirston]] ** [[Ortho]], the homeworld of the [[Harmonium]] ** [[Qua-Nosham]] ** [[Ranais]] ** The [[Rock of Bral]] ** [[Rublia]] ** [[Terras]] ** [[Tuimuhva]] ==Appendix== ===External Links=== * {{EW|Material Plane}} * {{FRW}} * {{RW}} === Background Information === In 1st Edition (q.v. {{b|D&D|Manual of the Planes}}), the term "Prime" was used as "Primary" -- seeming to imply only the campaign world an individual group was using. In a Forgotten Realms game, [[Toril]] and its environs would be the "Prime" Material Plane, while another world like Krynn might be an "Alternate" Material Plane. With the introduction of 2nd Edition, and [[Spelljammer]] setting placing each campaign world within their own crystal sphere floating in phlogiston, "Prime Material" terminology expanded to include every known world. 3rd Edition seems to have banked on the original definition, and simply used "Material Plane," dropping the "Prime" part, but subsequent editions have included it once again. ===References=== {{Refs}} ===Connections=== {{Material plane}} {{Cosmologies}} [[Category:Locations]] [[Category:Planes of existence]] [[Category:Locations on Yggdrasil]]

The One and the Prime does not give 'quotes'.|Primus to a record keeper of the [[Fraternity of Order]]{{Cite book/The Great Modron March|12}}}} ==Description== Primus appeared as a large being—sometimes in a form of an androgynous [[gold]]-skinned [[humanoid]] with an face of emotionless expression. While in Mechanus, its body remained half-submerged in an energy pool within the center of the [[Great Modron Cathedral]]. Primus' form was connected to the expansive interface network known as the ''Infinity Web''. Primus' hands always remained unseen. Its right hand was obscured by vibrant, rainbow hued radiance, and the left was shrouded in black clouds. The Supreme Modron retained much of its form after it was slain and reborn as a [[vestige]]. As Primus was no longer bound to the ''Infinity Web'' and its energy pool, its humanoid form manifested atop a floating platform of a [[bronze]] seal, intricately linked to cogs, gears, and other revolving machinery. ==Personality== Primus was a manifestation of perfect logic and strict order. It was linked with the plane of Mechanus and they shared the same goals and actions. While some believed it only concerned itself with the plane's modrons, others believed Primus sought to extend perfect law and order throughout the entirety of the [[multiverse]].{{Cite book/Monster Manual 5th edition|224}} It absolutely detested the [[tanar'ri]] of the [[Abyss]], and held similar, if not as intense, enmity for the [[baatezu]] of the [[Nine Hells]].{{Cite book/Hellbound: The Blood War/The Dark of the War|69}} ==Abilities== [[File:Monodrone-5e.jpg|thumb|right|300px|''Primus was the divine creator of Mechanus' monodrones.]] Primus was considered a greater [[deity]] in Mechanus. Its power over the modrons was absolute. Nearly all modrons obeyed the orders of Primus and carried out its plans, save for those that were disconnected from Primus' network and went 'rogue'.{{Cite book/Acquisitions Incorporated|134}} Despite its immense power while in Mechanus, Primus was incapable of dispatching [[avatar]]s to other planes of existence. It could however instantly transport any being it touched to either [[Arcadia]] or [[Acheron]], by mere touch of its right or left hand respectively. Primus itself was entirely immune to [[magic]]. While Primus held the powers of a god, it was not immortal and could still be killed. Whenever slain, the highest-ranking [[secundus]] modron was promoted to its position and became the new Primus. ==Possessions== Primus had access to the [[Grand Orrery]], an elaborate and complex device that calculated the changes between the heavenly bodies of space, the numerous [[planes of existence]], and the infinite powers of the cosmos. ==Activities== The One and Prime established the rules and laws that governed all of Mechanus and its inhabitants. Through its supervision of the modrons, Primus maintained near-perfect order within the plane. Primus could issue to each modron telepathic commands and perceive the plane through their eyes, by means of the ''Infinity Web''.{{Cite book/The Great Modron March|11-13}} Primus was often subtle in its maneuvering, arranging for events that would cause its followers to take actions that were deemed most suitable.{{Cite book/Hellbound: The Blood War/The Dark of the War|69}} Due to the fact many modrons died in the [[lower planes]] during their [[Great Modron March]]es, Primus sought a solution to lessening their casualties as a result of the eternal [[Blood War]].{{Cite book/Hellbound: The Blood War/The Dark of the War|33}} ==Worshipers== While there were no known cults of Primus within Mechanus, it was worshipped as a deity by modrons. Primus was capable of creating new [[monodrone]]s and could grant any modron divine powers. As a vestige, Primus was capable of attracting [[binder]]s, spellcasters that gained powers from powerful extra-planar beings. ==History== [[File:Primus and Tenebrous-2e.jpg|thumb|right|300px|''Primus confronted by Tenebrous in the Great Modron Cathedral.'']] At some point in existence, Primus created a massive stone crafted in complex geometry known as the ''[[Spawning Stone]]'' and imbued it with the essence of law itself. It then cast it into the plane of [[Limbo]], believing it would cure its chaotic nature and establish some form of order. This act had an effect that was diametrically opposed to Primus' original intent: it led to the creation of the [[slaad]]i race. The Slaadi then proceeded to annihilate every modron outpost within all of Limbo.{{Cite adventurers league/The Harrowing of Hell|29}} Primus was said to have once adjudicated the trial of [[Asmodeus]], when he was accused of horrific atrocities by the [[angel]]s of [[Celestia]]. In the end, Primus did not find wholly in favor of either party. Rather he rebuked the celestial angels and ensured Asmodeus would always have to be bound to the force of law.{{Cite book/Mordenkainen's Tome of Foes|9-10}} The One and Prime and its distinguished position among the modrons were known in the Realms since at least since {{Yearlink|-346}}. It was that year the plane of Mechanus was discovered by the [[Netherese]] [[archmage]], Lady [[Polaris]].>{{Cite book/How the Mighty Are Fallen|3, 31}} Primus was killed by [[Tenebrous]]—the dark [[vestige]] created after the death of [[Orcus]]—during the [[demon lord]]'s quest for divinity. Tenebrous then temporarily took over its position as head of the modrons, and initiated an unscheduled Modron March in order to recover his lost ''[[Wand of Orcus]]''.{{Cite book/Dead Gods|8-9}}{{Cite book/Dead Gods|37}} While the role of Primus was replaced by one of its [[Secundus|secundi]], the mind of the previous Primus remained present in the [[multiverse]] in the form of a [[vestige]].{{cite dragon/341/The Ties that Bind|72-73}} ==Appendix== ===Notes=== {{Notes}} ===Appearances=== :;Adventures ::''[[The Great Modron March]]'' • ''[[Dead Gods]]'' :;Card Games ::''[[Blood Wars]]'' :;Organized Play & Licensed Adventures ::{{Refonly}} ::[[Adventurers League/Dreams of the Red Wizards|Dreams of the Red Wizards]] (''[[The Harrowing of Hell]]'') ===Gallery=== Image:Primus.jpg|Concept art for 5{{th}} edition Primus, by [[Conceptopolis]] ===Further reading=== *{{Cite web enhancement/The Modrons}} *{{Cite dragon/341/The Ties that Bind}} ===References=== {{Refs}} ===Connections=== {{Modrons}} [[Category:Inhabitants of unspecified gender]] [[Category:Modrons]] [[Category:Rulers]] [[Category:Deities]] [[Category:Greater deities]] [[Category:Vestiges]] [[Category:Lawful neutral deities]] [[Category:Inhabitants of Regulus]] [[Category:Inhabitants of Mechanus]] [[Category:Inhabitants of the Outer Planes]] [[Category:Inhabitants of the Great Wheel planes]] [[Category:Inhabitants]] [[Category:Monster|Modron, 1]]

It was created and ruled by the [[archfey]] [[Zybilna]], an alias of the [[Oerth]]ian [[archmage]] [[Tasha]].<ref name="WBW-p171" /><ref name="WBW-p215">{{Cite book/The Wild Beyond the Witchlight|215}}</ref>
{{Quote|This is all very odd. This doesn't feel like Prismeer at all...Zybilna can't possibly be in charge anymore|[[Ellywick Tumblestrum]], venturing into the warped forest of [[Thither]].<ref name="ICFR">{{Cite game/Idle Champions of the Forgotten Realms}}</ref>}}
==Description== Like other domains within the Feywild, Prismeer's appearance shifted depending on the emotions of those that dwelled within. Zybilna herself could reshape all of Prismeer with a dramatic shift in her feelings, while her period of dormancy allowed others to alter the domain to their own will.<ref name="WBW-p60">{{Cite book/The Wild Beyond the Witchlight|60}}</ref>
Following its takeover by a [[coven]] of [[hag]]s, Prismeer was split into three distinct realms: the lurking swamp of [[Hither]], the ancient woods of [[Thither]], and the perilous mountains of [[Yon]]. Each of the realms were separated from the others by obstructive walls of mist, similar to those that surrounded the domain as a whole.<ref name="WBW-p57-58">{{Cite book/The Wild Beyond the Witchlight|57-58}}</ref>
===Magic=== Any children that entered into Prismeer―whether intentionally, inadvertently, or otherwise―were protected by magic enchantments created by Zybilna. It was noteworthy that children never seemed to age within Prismeer, regardless of how long they dwelled within.<ref name="WBW-p60" />
Death played out different in Prismeer than it did on the [[Prime Material plane]]. In some instances, a creature's body could decay in here moments or turn to stone after its death. In others, the remains could be ''[[gentle repose|placed into a form of stasis]]'' or ''[[revivify|instantly rejuvinated]]'', albeit in a weakened state.<ref name="WBW-p60" />
===Laws=== Prismeer was bound by a set of laws forged by Zybilna, to which every living being within was subject: * The '''Rule of Hospitality''', which stated everyone was required to be welcoming and congenial to anyone that entered into their home, unless they demonstrated they were unworthy of such accommodation.<ref name="WBW-p57-58" /> * The '''Rule of Ownership''', which forbade thievery or burglary of any kind.<ref name="WBW-p57-58" /> * The '''Rule of Reciprocity''', which directed that anyone receiving of a gift was expected to return the gesture in kind, even if in the distant future.<ref name="WBW-p57-58" />
Failure to adhere to Zybilna's three rules led to excommunication from Prismeer.<ref name="WBW-p57-58" />
==Cosmography== Like other Domains of Delight, Prismeer was bound entirely within the Feywild. It was confined within great walls of mists, passage through was was only granted by express consent of the domain's ruling archfey.<ref name="WBW-p57-58" />
The ancient forests of Prismeer held numerous ''[[faerie ring]]s'' that were ''[[fey crossroad]]s'' that bound Prismeer to various worlds in different [[crystal sphere]]s,<ref name="WBW-p99">{{Cite book/The Wild Beyond the Witchlight|99}}</ref> and one within the [[Witchlight Carnival]].<ref name="WBW-p23">{{Cite book/The Wild Beyond the Witchlight|23}}</ref>
==Notable Locations== [[File:Palace_of_Heart's_Desire.jpg|thumb|right|300px|''The Palace of Heart's Desire, Zybilna's home in the center of Prismeer.'']] * [[Palace of Heart's Desire]], Zybilna's personal refuge that attracted wayward mortal visitors from across the [[multiverse]].<ref name="WBW-p171">{{Cite book/The Wild Beyond the Witchlight|171}}</ref>
==History== At some point in time, control over Prismeer was stripped from Zybilna from her three hag stepsisters, known collectively as the [[Hourglass Coven]]. The coven split the domain into three distinct realms, each of which one of the sisters claimed as their own.<ref name="WBW-p99" />

'''Ptah''' was a Lesser Power of the [[Pharaonic pantheon]] and a god of craftsmen and travelers. According to legend, he predated even [[Ra]] but stepped down in favour of the stronger power. He wandered the [[Ethereal plane|Ethereal Plane]] and was one of the few powers approachable by mortals, but he was known to fling those who displeased him across the planes. His worshippers included artisans and craftsmen who desired inspiration in creating beauty.<ref>{{Cite book/On Hallowed Ground|90}}</ref>
Ptah's name was commonly invoked by travelers of the [[Inner Planes]]. It was believed that his inspiration allowed planewalkers to cross the harsh elemental landscapes more easily than those of the [[Outer Planes]].<ref>{{Cite book/On Hallowed Ground|46}}</ref>
In the year −2488 by the Faerûn calendar,<ref>{{Cite book/The Grand History of the Realms|18}}</ref> Ptah led the Pharaonic deities to assist the [[Mulhorand|Mulhorandi]] people in overthrowing their enslavers, the Imaskar Empire.<ref>{{Cite book/Powers & Pantheons|94}}</ref>

==Description== Quadrones were cube-shaped and winged.<ref name="MM5e-p224,226" /><ref name="MM21e-p88" /> Though some older versions were known to have a second set of arms in place of wings.<ref name="MM21e-p88" />
==Personality== Like all modrons, quadrones had an absolute sense of hierarchy and order, and could not be persuaded to disobey their instructions or betray their purpose in any way.<ref name="MM5e-p224,226" /><ref name="MM21e-p86">{{Cite book/Monster Manual II (1983)|86}}</ref>
It was possible, however, for a defective quadrone to go rogue and start acting in its own interests or no longer in accordance with its instructions, sometimes even becoming violent. Such rogues were relentlessly hunted by other modrons, although, unlike their properly operating fellows, they could be reasoned with.<ref name="MM5e-p224,226" /><ref name="MM21e-p87">{{Cite book/Monster Manual II (1983)|87}}</ref>
==Biology== On all six sides of their bodies were sensory organs far superior to that of any [[human]]. These granted them<ref name="MM21e-p88" /> [[True seeing|truesight]],<ref name="MM5e-p224,226" /> in addition to being able to view the [[Infravision|infrared]] and [[Ultravision|ultraviolet spectrums]] out to {{SI|180|ft|long=yes}} and {{SI|200|yards|long=yes}}, respectively. These senses enabled them to rarely be surprised by opponents.<ref name="MM21e-p88" />
==Abilities== Like all modrons, quadrones were immune to all effects and spells that influenced the mind, fear and attacks that rely on energy from either the [[Negative Energy plane|Negative]] or [[Positive Energy plane|Positive]] energy planes. They also had a resistance to acid, cold and fire.<ref name="TGMM">{{Cite book/The Great Modron March|126}}</ref>
Unlike tridones and other lower ranked modrons, these creatures had four complete functions<ref name="MM21e-p88" /> and thus were capable of performing four simultaneous tasks at a time.<ref name="MM5e-p224,226" /> These functions typically included being able to report actions as well as observations, devise plans, react to situations that were unexpected, and act in accordance to solve those situations.<ref name="MM21e-p88" />
==Combat== Quadrones were capable of wielding weapons and were exceptionally proficient with bows, with which they capable of performing four attacks at a time. If destroyed, a quadrone disintegrated completely into dust and a [[tridrone]] was instantly upgraded into a quadrone to fill its position.<ref name="MM5e-p224,226" />
==Society== [[File:Rogue-quadrone-5e.jpg|thumb|250px|''A rogue quadrone.'']] Quadrones could communicate with other quadrones and with [[tridrone]]s and [[pentadrone]]s. They were incapable of communicating directly with lesser modrons and could not comprehend any of the hierarch modrons, such as [[decaton]]s.<ref name="MM5e-p224,226" />
In modron society, they were responsible for supervising other groups of modrons, as well as performing services as multifunctional laborers.<ref name="MotPWE3e-p2">{{Cite web enhancement/The Modrons|2}}</ref> During battles they often served the role of a field officer.<ref name="MM21e-p88" /> They were always created as the result of tridrones being upgraded to take the place of destroyed or further upgraded units.<ref name="MM5e-p224,226" />
There were approximately one and and a half million quadrones in modron society at any time.<ref name="MM21e-p86">{{Cite book/Monster Manual II (1983)|86}}</ref> During battles, a regiment would typically feature a dozen of the best quadrones available.<ref name="MM21e-p88" />
==Notable Quadrones== * [[Halastron]], a rogue quadrone adopted by [[Halaster Blackcloak]] who lived in the [[Arcane Chambers]] level of [[Undermountain]].<ref name="WDMM5e-p41">{{Cite book/Waterdeep: Dungeon of the Mad Mage|41}}</ref> * [[Nordom]], a rogue quadrone and companion of the [[Nameless One]].<ref>{{Cite game/Planescape: Torment}}</ref>

==Description== Quartons were very tall humanoids, with a height of {{SI|12|ft}}. From their back grew two large wings that resembled fans. They had four arms with multiple joints.<ref name="MotPWE3e-p14-15" />
==Combat== If forced into combat, quartons used a combination of innate abilities, spells, tail and their fists.
==Abilities== Like all hierarch modrons, quartons had the innate ability to duplicate the effects of ''[[clairaudience]]'', ''[[clairvoyance]]'', ''[[command]]'', ''[[dimension door]]'', ''[[teleport without error]]'', and ''[[wall of force]]'' spells at will.<ref name="TGMM">{{Cite book/The Great Modron March|126}}</ref> Quartons were able to cast [[arcane]] spells as well as [[divine]] spells from the [[Law domain|Law]], [[Protection domain|Protection]] and [[War domain|War]] domains. Quartons were immune to all effects that influenced the mind, all psionic-based attacks and had a resistance to acid, cold and fire.<ref name="MotPWE3e-p14-15" />

Each quarton had a personal staff of these hierarchs attached to his staff, plus thirty-six [[pentadrone]]s who acted as a guard unit.<ref name="MMII1-.<p90">{{Cite book/Monster Manual II 1st edition|90}}</ref>
==Ecology== Quartons were able to communicate telepathically with any sentient creature within {{SI|405|mi|k}} and could see in [[darkvision]] up to {{SI|60|ft}}.

It was a place that sucked the warmth from any living creature.<ref name="TIP-pp108-113" /><ref name="PCS-ADMGttP-p37" /><ref name="MotP1e-p58" />
==Description== In most areas of this plane the ash had the consistency of hard-packed soil, though in some regions it was much less dense.<ref name="TIP-p9">{{Cite book/The Inner Planes|9}}</ref>
The cooling cinders within the air of this plane sucked the warmth from not only living creatures, but from magical effects as well. This made long term [[spell]]s such as ''[[heat metal]]'' and ''[[wall of fire]]'' ineffective on this plane. These cinders also gradually deteriorated the health of creatures of [[elemental fire]] and magma.<ref name="PCS-p37">{{Cite book/Planescape Campaign Setting/A DM Guide to the Planes|37}}</ref>
==History== Records found inside of an abandoned citadel on the world of [[Oerth]] hint that a community of [[dwarves]] may have tried to establish a colony in this plane, though their fate was unknown.<ref name="TIP-p111-112">{{Cite book/The Inner Planes|111-112}}</ref>
==Notable Locations== Other than the core of Ash, the regions of the quasiplane are measured by their proximity to other Inner Planes.
* The '''[[Citadel of Former Flame]]''': the home of [[Gazra (archomental)|Gazra]], a creature who claimed to be the [[archomental]] of the plane, and the capital of the [[ash quasi-elemental]] empire. A variety of undead guarded the citadel including [[ghoul]]s, [[spectre]]s, and [[wraith]]s. The citadel itself was made from the very ash of this plane, carved and magically fused together, and was constantly altering its form in a gradual manner. Inside it was devoid of both heat and light. Both mundane and [[magic]]al forms of illumination wouldn't function within it.<ref name="TIP-p112" />
=== [[Wasting Place]] ===
The border between Ash and the [[Quasi-Elemental Plane of Dust]].
=== [[Cinder Wells]] ===
The border between Ash and the [[Fountains of Creation|Paraelemental Plane of Magma]].
=== [[Sea of Frozen Flames]] ===
The border between Ash and the [[Elemental Plane of Fire]].
=== [[Embers]] ===
The border between Ash and the [[Great Conflagration|Paraelemental Plane of Smoke]].
=== [[Sparkling Vast]] ===
The border between Ash and the [[Quasi-Elemental Plane of Vacuum]].
=== [[Empty Winter]] ===
The border between Ash and the [[Negative Energy plane]].
* [[Citadel Cavitius]]: a massive skull-shaped fortress that was constructed by the [[Doomguard]] and later taken from them by [[Vecna]], who partially repurposed the stronghold as a prison.<ref name="PCS-p37" /> * The [[Crumbling Citadel]]: Once Cavitius was taken by Vecna, the Doomguard built a replacement citadel. It's constantly in the process of falling apart, and no one's quite sure why, but the Doomguard at least seem to enjoy constantly rebuilding it and shoring it up.
==Inhabitants== The two most predominant sentient species on this plane were [[ash mephit]]s and ash quasi-elementals. The former lived in scattered communities, while the latter had a substantial empire centered around the Citadel of Former Flame.<ref name="TIP-p111">{{Cite book/The Inner Planes|111}}</ref>
There lived a roaming group of [[ghast]]s and ghouls on this plane, numbering in the hundreds, that were referred to as the '''Flesh Renders'''. Due to going great lengths of time without any sustenance, they were particularly savage [[undead]]. Some speculated that they may have once been minions of Vecna.<ref name="TIP-p112">{{Cite book/The Inner Planes|112}}</ref>

{{Plane | image = | caption = | name = Quasi-Elemental Plane of Radiance | othernames = | natives = | languages = | curtain-color = Shifting rainbow | fork-material = [[Copper]] | fork-note = A# | fork-audio = A4-sharp.ogg | basicrefs = <ref name="MotP1e-p12">{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 1st edition|12}}</ref><ref name="AGttEP-p20">{{Cite book/A Guide to the Ethereal Plane|20}}</ref><ref name="Dr120-pp42-43">{{Cite dragon/120/Plane Speaking|42-43}}</ref> | type-GW = [[Inner Plane]] | shape-size-GW = Infinite | gravity-GW = Subjective Directional | time-GW = Normal | morphic-GW = Alterable Morphic | element-energy-GW = | alignment-GW = Mildly chaos-aligned | magical-GW = | layers-GW = | layer-number-GW = | location-GW = | refs-GW = <ref name="PSIP2e-p100-103" /><ref name="MP3e-p68">{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 3rd edition|68}}</ref> | type-WA = | shape-size-WA = | gravity-WA = | mutability-WA = | element-energy-WA = | alignment-WA = | magical-WA = | layers-WA = | layer-number-WA = | location-WA = | refs-WA = | type-WT = | shape-size-WT = | gravity-WT = | time-WT = | morphic-WT = | element-energy-WT = | alignment-WT = | magical-WT = | faith-WT = | layers-WT = | layer-number-WT = | location-WT = | refs-WT = | inhabitants = yes | deities = | locations = yes | organizations = | settlements = | usethe = yes | useon = }} The '''Quasi-Elemental Plane of Radiance''', also known simply as '''Radiance''', was an [[Inner Plane]] in the [[Great Wheel cosmology]].<ref name="PSIP2e-p100-103">{{Cite book/The Inner Planes|100-103}}</ref>
==Geography== Radiance stood at the border between the [[Elemental Plane of Fire]] and the [[Positive Energy plane]]. It was an extremely beautiful and overwhelmingly bright place, whose constant luminosity threatened to blind anyone who stared for too long.<ref name="PSIP2e-p9">{{Cite book/The Inner Planes|9}}</ref>
[[Portal]]s leading to Radiance resembled bright colorful rings of light that tended to be ephemeral and fickle, changing in and out of shape and leading to different locations within the plane.<ref name="PSIP2e-p100-103" />
Along the inner side of the [[crystal sphere]] of [[Realmspace]], there were numerous portals to Radiance that ranged between a few yards and hundreds of miles in diameter, that appeared at the dots and dashes of the strange writings that were marked on the surface of the sphere. These brilliant portals, thousands of miles apart from each other on the sphere's surface, were seen from the inhabitants of all the planets as stars and [[constellation]]s.<ref name="RS2e-p3-4">{{Cite book/Realmspace|3-4}}</ref>
Although Radiance was highly destructive to creatures and [[spelljammer]]s that dared enter it, portals through the sphere could be safely created on top of a star-opening, temporarily superseding it. For an inhabitant on one of the planets, that particular star would seem to disappear for a few minutes and then reappear.<ref name="RS2e-p3-4" />
The brilliance of the plane was blinding to unprotected visitors. Spells such as ''[[darkness]]'' were capable of offering protection and allowed visitors to see normally, providing only a weak shade.<ref name="MP1e-p55-56">{{Cite book/Manual of the Planes 1st edition|55-56}}</ref><ref name="PSIP2e-p100-103" />
The plane was as hot as the Plane of Fire,<ref name="MP1e-p55-56" /> so unprotected flammable materials would burst into flames within seconds. Liquids also boiled away into superheated steam. Not even [[magic item]]s were completely immune to the raw energy of the place. Creatures that lacked [[fire]] resistance needed magical protection from spells such as ''[[protection from energy]]'' or items such as ''[[ring of fire resistance|rings of fire resistance]]''. The atmosphere, however, was breathable.<ref name="PSIP2e-p100-103" />
Like the [[Elemental Plane of Air]], Radiance did not possess a solid ground and its gravity was subjective to an individual's perception.<ref name="PSIP2e-p100-103" />
==Notable Locations== Near the boundary with the [[Quasi-Elemental Plane of Lightning]], multicolored storms could throw creatures enormous distances away. A small island known as the [[Refuge of Color]] was the only naturally occurring solid ground on the plane.<ref name="PSIP2e-p100-103" />
The main reason for visitors to go to Radiance was the [[Heart of Light]], a mysterious tower of blue light that stood near the boundary with the Positive Energy Plane.<ref name="PS2e-DM-p35">{{Cite book/Planescape Campaign Setting/A DM Guide to the Planes|35}}</ref> It was a place where injuries and wounds healed at a rapid pace, whose origins were unknown.<ref name="PSIP2e-p100-103" />
==Inhabitants== The Plane of Radiance had few native creatures. It was inhabited by [[radiance quasi-elemental]]s, [[radiant mephit]]s, [[darklight]]s, [[scile]], and [[varisoh]]. Most natives tended to be solitary thinkers and philosophers.<ref name="PS32e-p11,84">{{Cite book/Monstrous Compendium Planescape Appendix III|11,84}}</ref>

==Description== Quintons were tall yet heavyset humanoid with four arms and a prehensile tail, all of which sported a five-fingered hand. They had a pair of wings that resembled fans on their backs. Upon their forehead was a diamond symbol, which denoted their rank.<ref name="MotPWE3e" />
==Combat== If forced into combat, quintons used a combination of innate abilities, spells and their fists.<ref name="MotPWE3e" />
==Abilities== Like all hierarch modrons, quintons had the innate ability to duplicate the effects of ''[[clairaudience]]'', ''[[clairvoyance]]'', ''[[command]]'', ''[[dimension door]]'', ''[[teleport without error]]'', and ''[[wall of force]]'' spells at will.<ref name="TGMM">{{Cite book/The Great Modron March|126}}</ref> Quintons were able to cast [[divine]] spells from the [[Law domain|Law]], [[Protection domain|Protection]] and [[War domain|War]] domains. Quintons were immune to all effects that influenced the mind, all psionic-based attacks and had a resistance to acid, cold and fire.<ref name="MotPWE3e" />
==Society== There were exactly twenty-five quintons in modron society—one stationed at each of the twenty bureaus in the region and quarter towers, and five in the bureaus at [[Primus Tower]] at the capital. They acted as the bureau chiefs and record keepers of [[Mechanus|Nirvana]].<ref name="MMII1e-p90" />
Each quinton had one [[hexton]] assistant,<ref name="MotPWE3e-p14-15" /> plus a staff of one [[septon]], twenty-five [[pentadrone]]s, sixty-four [[quadrone]]s, eighty-one [[tridrone]]s, and an unknown number of [[duodrone]]s and [[monodrone]]s.<ref name="MMII1e-p90" />
==Ecology== Quintons were able to communicate telepathically with any sentient creature within {{SI|238|mi|k}} and could see in [[darkvision]] up to {{SI|60|ft}}.<ref name="MotPWE3e" />
==History== The [[Great Modron March]], the periodic tour of the [[Outer Planes]] carried out once every 289 years, was led by a quinton, who was also the chief record-keeper of the voyage.<ref name="GMM2e-p8">{{Cite book/The Great Modron March|8}}</ref> The march passed briefly through [[Undermountain]], using one of the rare ''[[portal]]s'' that led out of [[Carceri]].<ref name="GMM2e-p91">{{Cite book/The Great Modron March|91}}</ref>

{{Deity|name=Ra|title=Pharaoh of the Gods|symbol=Ankh on a solar disc|power=Greater Power|pantheon=[[Pharaonic pantheon]]|gender=Masculine|realm=[[Thekele-Re]], [[Heliopolis]]|portfolio=The sun, kings|worshipers=|cleric alignments=Lawful|alignment=Lawful Good}} '''Ra''' was a Greater [[Power]] and leader of the [[Pharaonic pantheon]], who brought forth the Ennead and raised many of the other Pharaonic powers to divinity.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book/On Hallowed Ground|84}}</ref> He was symbolised in Egyptian and Mulhorandi culture as a human with the head of a falcon.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book/On Hallowed Ground|86}}</ref> In the Mulhorandi interpretation of the pantheon, his personality and sphere were combined with those of [[Horus]] and worshipped as '''Horus-Re''', who was sometimes interpreted as Ra's son.<ref>{{Cite book/Faiths & Pantheons|143||chapter=}}</ref>
Ra was known as the original Pharaonic deity, who brought life to the rest of his extended family, the Ennead. He was one of the first to understand the power of the [[Three Truths|Rule of Threes]], and created eight other gods to rule with him for a three-threes structure. Rumours claimed that [[Ptah]] was the original head of the pantheon, or that another group called the Eight Fathers and Mothers predate even him, but the truth of this was lost to time.<ref name=":0" />
Ra ruled the First Realm of [[Heliopolis]], [[Thekele-Re]], where he brought light to the world with his solar barge [[Matet|''Manjet'']]. He guided the pharaohs of Mulhorand, Egypt and countless other civilisations, and protected them from the world-destroyer serpent [[Apophis]]. The chant went that as Apophis stirred once again, Ra was preparing to move onto "bigger and better things", and had his second-in-command [[Osiris]] lined up to take over the pantheon.<ref name=":1" />

'''Ranais''', "the Funereal World," is the primary inhabited world found within an unknown crystal sphere on the [[Prime Material plane]].<ref name="dg28">{{b|Planescape|Dead Gods|pdf=17297|page=28}}</ref> The world was subject to some form of calamity centuries ago. It was often used as a quick way to travel between [[Crux]] and [[Sigil]]: the portals were only about 15 miles apart, through the ruins of a once-great city.
The sun is tiny and white, providing little in the way of warmth or illumination. As a result, even during daytime, the effect is that of constant night.
The population revered death in many forms (although they were unconnected to the [[Heralds of Dust]]), including [[Orcus]]. When the city of Moil turned away from Orcus, he cast it into a demiplane, and the rest of the world was plunged into chaos. Those who could, escaped to other planes, the rest perishing, haunting the world as a form of spirit called the [[Lovelost]].
When Orcus returned as [[Tenebrous]], he commanded his servants, the [[visage]]s, use the ruins of Ranais as their base of operations, specifically the ruins of a Temple of Orcus.<ref name="dg52">{{b|Planescape|Dead Gods|pdf=17297|page=52}}</ref>
== Personalities ==
Centuries ago, refugees from Ranais fled to the planes. Many settled into the town of [[Crux]] on [[Yggdrasil]], while others settled in their own neighborhood in [[Sigil]], which they call [[Goatswood]]. It was originally in the Lower Ward, but as ward boundaries shifted, Goatswood is now considered part of the [[Hive Ward]].<ref name="fw27">{{b|Planescape|Faction War (book)|alt=Faction War|pdf=17299|page=27}}</ref>
== Portals ==
The following portals are known to link to Ranais:
* From High Point in [[Crux]] to Ranais. The portal was always open, resembling a [[color pool]].<ref name="dg47">{{b|Planescape|Dead Gods|pdf=17297|page=47}}</ref><ref name="dg51">{{b|Planescape|Dead Gods|pdf=17297|page=51}}</ref> The portal closed following the return of Orcus, cutting Crux off from both their ancestral homeworld and also Sigil.<ref name="dg124">{{b|Planescape|Dead Gods|pdf=17297|page=124}}</ref> * A set of double-doors on a stable in the [[Market Ward]] to Ranais.<ref name="dg51">{{b|Planescape|Dead Gods|pdf=17297|page=51}}</ref> * To the fortress of [[Tcian Sumere]] in the [[Negative Energy plane]] from the Temple of Orcus. The portal (and the whole temple) vanished once Orcus returned.<ref name="dg124">{{b|Planescape|Dead Gods|pdf=17297|page=124}}</ref>
== Gods ==
The people of Ranais venerated many gods of death, including (but not limited to) Orcus. Each major city had their own patron god.
